A1.justification: Despite the changed title and organization, both PDFs describe the same research on distributional associations, attention, and weight truncation. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original GPT-2/Pythia evaluations, noisy-recall transformer experiments, architectural ablations, and repeated associative-memory simulations.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds GSM8K evaluations, parameter-allocation experiments, expanded Pythia results, and synthetic IOI counting experiments.

M1.justification: The simplified analytical model now combines current-token and separate previous-token embeddings (v2 Equation 2), whereas v1 Section 3.1 uses current-token embeddings alone. This changes the analyzed input model. The experimental two-layer architecture, cross-entropy objective, and SVD truncation procedure remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds GSM8K mathematical word problems and a synthetic IOI task requiring discrimination between a target occurring once and a distractor occurring twice (Appendix J). These substantially extend task requirements beyond the retained noisy recall, factual recall, and preposition evaluations.

E2.justification: Comparisons remain between unmodified models and their rank-truncated or layer-removal variants. The new GSM8K backbones and deeper synthetic models extend this comparison design; they do not introduce a distinct competing editing or truncation method.

E3.justification: New protocols include 1/2/4/8-shot GSM8K evaluation, 3–7-layer synthetic models with SGD and 3–5-layer models with Adam, and fixed-budget parameter-allocation tests trained for 100 steps. Additional Pythia configurations and a 20-query factual evaluation are reported. The clean-pretraining caption is corrected from alpha=1 to alpha=0, without establishing a rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds fixed-budget MLP-versus-attention allocation analysis (Figure 6), a direct FF-2 noise-margin trajectory (Figure 3), and depth/optimizer/truncation analyses on synthetic IOI (Figures 19–20). Earlier multiple-trigger, architectural, and associative-memory ablations are retained under new numbering.

E5.justification: Figures 15–16 add distributional summaries of prediction variability across IOI and factual prompts, supplementing the earlier averages and single-prompt presentation. These describe variation across inputs. Associative-memory reporting remains 20 runs with median and 25th/75th percentiles; no increased repeated-run count or new significance testing is stated.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for GSM8K, parameter allocation, Pythia prediction distributions, and synthetic counting. New Table 2 reports Phi-3 accuracy of 56.0% versus 66.1% with LASER at one shot, but 82.7% versus 82.3% at eight shots. Appendix J also reports five-layer Adam nonconvergence. These are additional evaluations, not improvements over v1 under identical settings.

T1.justification: New Theorem 2 and Appendix F develop a three-phase argument for attention preferring correct successors over noise, with orthogonality, population-gradient, and noise-level assumptions. This extends v1's exploratory noise-avoidance calculation, retained as Appendix B.3. The associative-memory theorem is retained as Theorem 3, and Lemma H.1 gains a population-gradient derivation.

C1.justification: The central separation claim persists. v2 strengthens the stated contribution from a standalone noisy associative-memory result to explaining separation within attention value matrices when feed-forward layers are absent. The introduction also incorporates theoretical target selection into its account of early training.

C2.justification: v2 connects associative memory to attention without feed-forward layers and adds implications for parameter allocation, circuit discovery, and selective fine-tuning. It discusses shot-dependent GSM8K benefits and attributes possible Adam instability to missing normalization. Conversely, Section 5 removes v1's specific open questions about attention sinks/registers and joint SGD dynamics.

D1.justification: v2 supplies an implementation link, explains the existing clean-pretraining/noisy-fine-tuning procedure, adds model-specific LASER settings, and documents the new factual prompts and synthetic IOI generation. The earlier SGD, batch-size, dimensionality, V100 hardware, and training-time disclosures remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including Chan, Akyürek, Mahankali, and an additional Sanford work, alongside citations supporting the new benchmark, models, and optimizer. Darcet and Xiao references disappear with the attention-sink/register discussion. Positioning relative to LASER and Bietti's transformer analysis remains substantially intact.

P1.justification: The title and abstract are rewritten, terminology shifts from global to distributional associations, and LLM experiments move from motivation to a dedicated Section 4. Linear associative memory becomes Section 3.3, appendices are reorganized, and the conclusion is substantially shortened.

P2.justification: v2 adds conceptual schematics, expands Figure 3 with a margin panel, and introduces GSM8K and factual-input tables plus allocation, distribution, and synthetic-task plots. Existing displays are relocated, including v1's GPT-2 Figure 1 becoming appendix Figure 17. Conference formatting substantially reflows the document.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central mechanistic account through a conditional attention target-selection theorem and fixed-budget controls. Counting and GSM8K evaluations address the earlier reliance on simpler tasks, while adverse shot-dependent results and Adam failure clarify applicability. Schematics and implementation information improve accessibility. The theory remains idealized and specific limitations are shortened, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the stronger explanatory and empirical support.
